prompt: Let $A$ be a set and $R\subseteq A\times A$ a binary relation on $A$. For $x,y\in A$, write $R(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in R$. Which condition defines antitransitivity? Here antitransitive means that every two-step chain lacks its shortcut.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(y,z))\Rightarrow\neg R(x,z))$.
answers.explanation: Every two-step chain lacks its direct shortcut. Failure of transitivity instead requires at least one chain without its shortcut.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(y,z))\Rightarrow R(x,z))$.
answers.explanation: Every two-step chain has its direct shortcut, including chains with repeated vertices. This defines transitivity, not antitransitivity.
Every related pair has its reverse; loops are allowed but not required. This defines symmetry, not antitransitivity.
Every element has a self-loop; pairs of different elements are unrestricted. This defines reflexivity, not antitransitivity.

answers.text: $\exists x\in A\;\exists y\in A\;\exists z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(y,z))\land\neg R(x,z))$.
answers.explanation: Some two-step chain lacks its shortcut; other chains may have shortcuts. This defines failure of transitivity, not antitransitivity.
No element has a self-loop; pairs of different elements are unrestricted. This defines irreflexivity, not antitransitivity.
Every related pair has no reverse. Taking the two elements equal also forbids loops. This defines asymmetry, not antitransitivity.
No ordered pair is present, including between distinct elements. This defines emptiness, not antitransitivity.
Some related pair lacks its reverse; this is an existential violation. This defines failure of symmetry, not antitransitivity.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(x,z))\Rightarrow y=z)$.
answers.explanation: An element has at most one outgoing related element; it need not have any. This defines right-uniqueness, not antitransitivity.
